newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese foreign minister ordered back from Peru.
newsitem.headline: Japanese foreign minister ordered back from Peru.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Sunday ordered his foreign minister to return from Peru and predicted the hostage crisis in Lima would take a considerable time to resolve.

Hashimoto threw Japan's full support behind the tough line that Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori has adopted towards negotiations to free the some 340 hostages, and said the ball was now in the guerrillas' court.
"A considerable time would be needed to resolve (the crisis)," Hashimoto told reporters. He did not elaborate.
The hostage crisis began last Tuesday night when the Peruvian Marxist guerrillas seized the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

Hashimoto made his comments hours after a grim Fujimori told the guerrillas in a national television address that a non-violent "way out" would be possible if they surrendered their weapons and released their hostages.
"We think we are at a stage where we shift our demands from the safety of the hostages to the immediate release of the hostages," said Hashimoto.
"It is the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA)'s turn to respond. Japan supports President Fujimori's televised message to the nation."
Hashimoto made his decision to bring Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda home after speaking by telephone with Ikeda, who hours earlier had a lengthy meeting with Fujimori.
"The proposal is concrete: that the captors surrender their weapons to a guarantor committee and that they allow the evacuation of all the hostages without exception," Fujimori said in his address.
"In this way the possibility of force being used by the Peruvian state will be ruled out and from there, with all guarantees, a way out can be studied."
The speech, which Fujimori read in a stern voice, was his first public statement since the crisis began when about 20 MRTA rebels stormed a cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's residence.
Japan's pledge of full support and Hashimoto's own tough words indicated Lima and Tokyo had agreed at last on how to handle the hostage situation.
Last Friday, Japan revealed there were wide differences between the governments.
Ikeda flew to Lima on Thursday as Japan's on-the-spot adviser on the crisis.
He held talks with Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, and Education Minister Domingo Palermo Cabrejos, who was acting as a negotiator for the release of the hostages.
Ikeda also met diplomats and consoled relatives of the dozens of Japanese diplomats and Peruvian-Japanese citizens held by the rebels.
After the second meeting with the Peruvian leader on Sunday, Ikeda said Tokyo fully backed Fujimori's tough address to the rebels.

"Although I cannot comment on the specifics, the proposal as a whole is the appropriate solution to a peaceful resolution to the crisis and the preservation of the lives of the hostages," Ikeda told Japanese reporters in Peru.
